blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Conversational Recommender Systems (CRSs) require reliable user simulators for cost-effective evaluation. LLM-based simulators have made realistic simulation possible but typically condition on profiles derived from explicit ratings, demographics, and static sources capturing surface preferences while omitting implicit behavioral characteristics such as decision-making style, aspect-level preferences, and domain expertise. We propose SimInter, a pipeline that elicits these attributes via synthetic interviews between two LLM agents, grounded in the user's statistical profile and historical conversational evidence. Before profile enrichment, an audit agent explicitly flags potential fabrication and stereotyping at the turn level. We instantiate and evaluate SimInter on movie recommendation. We simulate 300 ReDial users and, on a matched subset of 100 users, compare SimInter with a statistics-only baseline: SimInter significantly increases the diversity of expressed preference aspects (filtered aspect entropy: 1.619 vs. 0.859; paired d = 0.96, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). This gain persists when the simulator converses with two trained recommenders, KBRD and UniCRS, under two independent evaluation judges (+0.28 to +0.56 nats; all p < 0.001). Human evaluation finds 94.3% of enriched-attribute claims supported or partially supported, while human judgments agree with 95.2% of the auditor's binary filtering decisions on a stratified sample.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Conversational Recommender Systems (CRSs) have become a primary
interface for content
discovery Fu et al. (2020) ; Kim et al. (2012) , but their
evaluation remains difficult: studies with real users are expensive,
slow, and rarely reproducible, with outcomes depending on the specific
sample recruited Zhu et al. (2024b) . User simulation has
emerged as a complementary methodology in which artificial users
interact with a CRS in place of humans, enabling controlled, repeatable
experimentation at scale Balog and Zhai (2025) ; Zhu et al. (2024a) .

Early simulators were rule-based or agenda-based Ruß et al. (2012) ; Afzali et al. (2023) , offering controllability at the cost of behavioral
realism. Large language models (LLMs) have changed this picture, but
LLM-based simulators still exhibit characteristic failure modes:
repetitive responses, narrow choice ranges, binary reactions, and drift
toward generic “average user”
behavior Yoon et al. (2024) ; Zhu et al. (2024b) . We argue
that an important source of these limitations is the user profile that
conditions the simulator.

blocks.en:
Most LLM-based simulators condition generation on profiles built from
observable signals: ratings, interaction histories, and demographic
attributes. Such profiles capture what a user has consumed but
leave largely unspecified how the user makes choices: whether
they satisfice or maximize, whether their choices are driven by mood
or social context, and how willing they are to accept unfamiliar
recommendations. These behavioral dispositions strongly shape
conversational behavior yet are precisely what ratings-based profiles
omit Tigunova et al. (2019) ; Yoon et al. (2024) . A natural
alternative—prompting an LLM to infer behavioral attributes from a
static profile—has a known failure mode: LLMs tend to produce
stereotyped inferences, inflating apparent profile richness while
reducing individual fidelity. The same risk applies to self-play
dialogue, where two agents can amplify rather than reveal latent
attributes, fabricating plausible-sounding traits not grounded in
actual behavior.

blocks.en:
We propose SimInter , which derives behavioral attributes from
synthetic dialogue while explicitly defending against fabrication via
four design choices. (i) Statistical grounding : we first compute behavioral statistics
(acceptance rate, reference style, genre distribution, exploration
ratio) from the user’s interaction history; the synthetic dialogue
is then conditioned on these statistics and the user’s historical
conversational evidence. (ii) Interview rather than peer dialogue : generation is cast as
an asymmetric interview, with the interviewee anchored to the user’s
profile and the interviewer as a neutral elicitor probing specific
dimensions Tigunova et al. (2019) , preventing mutual
reinforcement of speculative content. (iii) Turn-level auditing : an Audit Agent flags fabrication, history contradictions, and caricature
(generic persona templates and invented rationalizations).
Depending on severity, flagged turns are excluded from
profile enrichment, while structurally compromised
dialogues trigger regeneration. (iv) Evidence-linked enrichment : an LLM agent enriches the
user’s statistical profile with attributes extracted from the audited
interview, with each categorical or scored attribute paired with a
supporting evidence quote; human annotators verify that 94 % 94\% of these
enriched claims are supported by the interview.

blocks.en: 3 Method
blocks.zh: 3 方法

blocks.en:
Figure 1 illustrates the SimInter pipeline.
The method consists of six stages:
(1) constructing basic user profiles from historical interactions,
(2) extracting behavioral statistics from these profiles,
(3) generating synthetic interviews between two LLM-based agents,
(4) auditing the generated conversations with an audit agent,
(5) extracting implicit user attributes and enriching the profiles,
and (6) simulating users interacting with a CRS using their
enriched profiles. We instantiate the LLM-based components with Gemini 2.5 Flash Comanici et al. (2025) for interview generation and user simulation, Claude Haiku 4.5 Anthropic (2025) for auditing, Tencent Hy3 Tencent Hy Team (2026) for enrichment,
and GPT-4o-mini Achiam et al. (2023) as the CRS the simulated user interacts with.
Models were chosen for availability and cost; where possible, we drew
components from different model families to reduce shared bias between
generator, auditor, and judges. All model choices are flexible.

blocks.en: 3.2 Synthetic Interview Generation
blocks.zh: 3.2 合成访谈生成

blocks.en: Stage 3 (Synthetic Interview Generation).
blocks.zh: 第3阶段(合成访谈生成).

blocks.en:
Conversations often contain implicit information that provides deeper
insights into
users Tigunova et al. (2019) ; Torbati et al. (2021) . We exploit LLMs’
role-playing capabilities Wang et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2024) to simulate interviews between two agents: an interviewee anchored to
the user’s profile and an interviewer that elicits it. For each of the
300 sampled users, the interviewee agent receives the user’s
statistical profile and one historical ReDial conversation in which
the user acts as a seeker. The interviewer, in contrast, has no access
to the profile or the ReDial history; it sees only the ongoing
interview, so that it cannot steer the interviewee toward known
preferences. It opens with one of four predefined open-ended
questions, chosen at random (e.g., “Walk me through the last
movie you really enjoyed — what was it and what stuck with you?” ;
all four are listed in Appendix J.1 ), and
dynamically adapts its follow-up questions to the interviewee’s
responses. Each interview comprises an initial six-turn elicitation
phase followed by four clarification turns, for a total of 10 turns.
Figure 3 shows an example; full system prompts
are in Appendix J .

blocks.en: 3.3 Conversation Auditing

blocks.en: Stage 4 (Conversation Auditing).

blocks.en:
An Audit Agent checks each interviewee turn against the
user’s own evidence, namely the statistical profile and the historical
ReDial conversation, for three types of issues. Fabrication covers specific claims that are neither stated in
nor plausibly inferable from this evidence, such as invented viewing
experiences or personal anecdotes. Caricature covers stereotyped persona performances and invented rationalizations : plausible-sounding justifications
for preferences that the profile does not attest, or recognizable
persona archetypes it does not support. History contradiction covers statements that conflict with the
user’s liked and disliked movies or with their earlier ReDial
conversation. In addition, deterministic structural checks verify the
number of turns, the alternation of speaker roles, and the absence of
empty turns.

blocks.en:
From audited interviews, we extract six implicit user attributes
grounded in prior user-modeling
literature: aspect-level
preferences Radlinski et al. (2019) , pickiness Yoon et al. (2024) , decision-making style Scott and Bruce (1995) ; Hayati et al. (2020) , viewing motivation Oliver and Raney (2011) , novelty preference Tang and Liao (2022) , and domain expertise Kostric et al. (2025) . Each attribute reveals
behavior not observable in the static profile: aspect preferences
organize preferences along Movie/Genre/Person/Other anchors; pickiness
captures selectivity; decision-making style ranges across rational,
intuitive, dependent, avoidant, and spontaneous; viewing motivation
combines a hedonic-eudaimonic score (1–5) with a primary category
(escapism, hedonic, eudaimonic, social, catharsis, arousal); novelty
preference scores openness to unfamiliar content (1–5); and domain
expertise classifies users as novice, intermediate, or cinephile.
Full attribute schemas, evidence-extraction prompts, and an example
enriched profile are in Appendix H .

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion

blocks.en:
We presented SimInter , a pipeline for LLM-based user simulation
that elicits qualitative behavioral attributes through structured
synthetic interviews and guards against fabrication via explicit
turn-level auditing. On 300 300 ReDial users, simulators conditioned on
enriched profiles discuss movies along substantially richer behavioral
aspects than a statistics-only baseline ( d z = 0.96 d_{z}=0.96 , p adj < 0.001 p_{\mathrm{adj}}<0.001 ; zero-aspect users drop from 41 % 41\% to 5 % 5\% );
pooled popularity alignment with MovieLens-25M reaches r = 0.347 r=0.347 ; and 94 % 94\% of enriched-attribute claims are human-supported. Enrichment
also concentrates item mentions and reduces lexical variety,
consistent with profile-conditioned generation narrowing expression
toward profile vocabulary. User-simulation quality in CRS is thus
multidimensional: the goal is not to maximize every diversity metric,
but to gain more on dimensions that matter for CRS evaluation than is
lost on those that do not.

blocks.en: Limitations
blocks.zh: 限制

blocks.en:
SimInter grounds enriched attributes in historical user
evidence, while independent validation against real
user behavior remains an important direction for
future work. Human evaluation assesses evidence
support rather than direct behavioral fidelity.
Moreover, audit decisions involve uncertainty,
particularly when distinguishing unsupported
rationalizations from legitimate preference
elaboration. Automatically retrieved evidence
and differences in annotator judgments further
limit conclusions about audit reliability.

blocks.en:
Our ablations do not include direct LLM-based
attribute inference without interviewing, leaving
the interview’s independent contribution unresolved.
Sparse and imbalanced preference evidence limits
individual-level alignment evaluation. Enrichment
also involves trade-offs between aspect richness,
item diversity, and lexical variety. Although
cross-CRS experiments support the robustness of
aspect-level findings, they rely on automated
evaluation and do not establish agreement with
real-user assessments of recommenders.
Generalization beyond English movie recommendation
remains to be investigated.
